Adult Oblique-banded grouper (Epinephelus radiatus) attain a maximum recorded total length of 70 cm [Li = 70 cm], a size that positions this species among the medium-bodied members of the Epinephelinae. This ultimate length is achieved through a growth trajectory influenced by the relatively stable thermal regime of their subtropical reef habitats. Field growth studies indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] when maintained under conditions typical of their natural environment, specifically a water temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. The corresponding asymptotic body mass derived from length-weight regressions yields an ultimate wet weight of approximately 9,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 9,700 grams], a figure that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to attain the largest sizes in the population. These life-history attributes suggest a comparatively slow pace of growth and maturation consistent with many epinephelid species inhabiting oligotrophic waters, where food availability constrains maximal size and longevity.

Female Oblique-banded grouper undergo sexual maturation at a total length of 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm], a relatively modest size compared to the species ultimate length. At this pubertal milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 230 grams [Wwp = 230 grams], derived from length-mass relationships established for the genus. This early maturation relative to maximum size indicates a life-history strategy that prioritizes initial reproductive output before reaching full somatic dimensions, a pattern common among protogynous hermaphrodites within the Epinephelidae. The initiation of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence at this stage is accompanied by measurable shifts in energy allocation, with females channeling resources toward egg production rather than continued rapid growth. Field observations confirm that individuals of approximately 21 cm in length are capable of participating in spawning aggregations, though their contribution to annual recruitment may be limited by their smaller body size and correspondingly lower fecundity compared to larger, more experienced females.

The reproductive output of the Oblique-banded grouper has been characterized under controlled conditions at a stable water temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce approximately 804 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 804 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the maximum reproductive capacity of the species under favorable environmental conditions. This daily fecundity estimate represents the product of spawning frequency and clutch size, with gravid individuals observed to release batches of eggs over an extended spawning season. The sustained production of pelagic eggs at this rate requires substantial energetic reserves, as each batch must be provisioned with yolk sufficient to support embryonic development through the early larval stages. Such high daily fecundity is typical of broadcast-spawning serranids that rely on larval drift and high mortality rates to regulate population size. The availability of zooplankton prey during the spawning period likely modulates whether females can sustain this peak output or must downregulate their reproductive effort in response to food limitation.

The embryonic stage of the Oblique-banded grouper begins with a fertilised ovum measuring approximately 0.6 mm in diameter, which upon eclosion yields a yolk-sac larva with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000113 grams [Wwb = 0.000113 grams]. This minute starting mass places the species among the many marine teleosts that produce numerous, small offspring as part of a classic r-selected early-life strategy, though adult traits such as delayed maturation and extended longevity lean toward K-selection. The yolk-dependent larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching, with the yolk-sac being progressively absorbed as the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. Mortality during this lecithotrophic phase is exceedingly high, with predation and starvation accounting for the vast majority of losses before individuals reach the first-feeding stage. The small size at birth also constrains the initial prey spectrum, as first-feeding larvae must capture appropriately sized zooplankton, typically copepod nauplii and rotifers, to successfully complete the trophic switch to exogenous feeding.

Comparative analyses within the genus Epinephelus reveal that the Oblique-banded grouper exhibits a life span of 15 years [am = 15 years] that is intermediate among its congeners, several of which may exceed three decades in cooler waters at a temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. However, at the species typical habitat temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C], metabolic rates are elevated, which may accelerate senescence relative to populations inhabiting cooler thermal regimes. This trade-off between temperature-driven metabolic demand and longevity is reflected in the species maximum recorded adult mass of 9,700 grams [Wwi = 9,700 grams], which is reached after approximately a decade of growth. The interplay between thermal conditions and body size also influences the timing of reproductive events, with first spawning typically occurring once females have surpassed the 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm] length threshold and accumulated sufficient energy reserves. These demographic parameters collectively suggest that population resilience in Epinephelus radiatus depends on maintaining adequate adult survivorship across multiple year classes, as reproductive output is distributed across a protracted adult lifespan rather than concentrated in a single season.
